sections.title: The tense of what you cannot check
sections.content: You know the future tense (*viajaré*, *viajará*) from A2 Unit 19, and the future for a guess about the present (*Estará en casa*) from B1 Unit 22. You also met the future perfect there: *habrá*, *habrás*, *habremos*... + the past participle. The B1 lesson only mentioned its second use: a guess about something that has already happened. Spanish uses the future for guesses because the future is the tense of what you cannot check yet, and a guess is exactly that. English says 'must be', 'probably' or 'I suppose'.

sections.title: Two tenses for guessing
rows: He is probably at home. (future: a guess about now)
He is probably sleeping. (estar in the future + gerund: a guess about what is going on now)
He has probably left already. (future perfect: a guess about what has happened)
Where can he be? (a question you ask yourself)

sections.title: Prediction or guess?
sections.content: The same future can predict or guess. *Llegará mañana* looks ahead, but *Estará en casa* is about now. Context decides: *mañana* points forward, *ya* and *ahora* point to now. With action verbs, use *estar* + gerund for a guess about what is happening now.

items.english: Marta is not answering; she is probably sleeping.

items.spanish: Tendrá unos cuarenta años, a juzgar por su aspecto.
items.english: She is probably about forty, judging by her appearance.
They have probably got home by now.
Where can I have left my keys?
It is probably half past nine.

sections.content: A guess in the future tense already says 'I am not sure', so you do not need an extra marker. If you are sure, use the present: *Está en casa*.
